results.result: A standardized decision-making task produces reproducible behavioral results across seven laboratories in three countries. After training 140 mice and collecting 5 million choices, once mice achieved proficiency, there were no significant differences in psychometric performance measures (lapse rates, contrast sensitivity, response bias) across laboratories (p>0.05 for all measures). Machine learning classifiers trained on behavioral variables failed to predict laboratory membership above chance level.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C109 provide strong statistical evidence that trained mouse behavior was indistinguishable across laboratories. Multiple psychometric measures showed no significant differences (C101-C102), within-lab consistency was not higher than across-lab (C103), and three different classifier algorithms failed to predict lab membership (C107-C109). The large sample size (140 mice, 5 million choices) and rigorous statistical testing support this major finding.

results.result: Learning speed varied substantially across mice and laboratories, with training times ranging from 3 to 59 days (mean 18.4±13.0 days) and 1,000 to 43,000 trials. The number of days to proficiency differed significantly across laboratories (p<0.001, Kruskal-Wallis test), with some labs showing homogeneous learning rates (interquartile range 8 days) and others showing high variability (interquartile range 22 days).
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C87 provide specific quantitative data on learning variability with appropriate statistical tests. The significant difference across laboratories (C83) is well-documented. However, the authors acknowledge they did not attempt to control this factor (C155) and can only speculate about causes (C156), which is appropriately transparent about limitations.

results.result: Mice across laboratories adopted similar decision-making strategies, showing comparable reliance on visual stimuli, past choices, and block priors. A generalized linear model revealed that visual weights grew with contrast to >3 at 100% contrast, while non-sensory factors had much lower weights. The shift in rightward choices at 0% contrast between block types (28.5%) did not differ significantly across laboratories (p=0.2455, one-way ANOVA). Model predictive accuracy was similar across laboratories (81-82%).
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C137 demonstrate that the GLM successfully captured decision strategies across laboratories with good predictive accuracy. The statistical tests (C120-C123) show consistent effects of block structure with no laboratory differences. The model's low condition numbers (C258-C260) indicate the coefficients are interpretable. This provides strong evidence for common decision-making strategies.

results.result: The study implemented a modified two-alternative forced-choice task where head-fixed mice turn a steering wheel to report the location of visual gratings presented at variable contrast. Training proceeded through automated steps with progressively introduced contrast levels (100%, 50%, 25%, 12%, 6%, 0%), adaptive wheel gain (8 to 4 deg/mm), and decreasing reward size (3 to 1.5 μL). The full task included blocks with asymmetric stimulus probabilities (20:80, 80:20, 50:50).
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C69 provide detailed, internally consistent descriptions of the task design and training procedures. The automated progression through contrast levels and parameter adjustments is well-documented. The task design is appropriate for studying decision-making and builds on established paradigms (supported by citations C27-C31).

results.result: The study standardized multiple experimental variables (mouse strain, age, weight, water access, food composition) while documenting but not standardizing others (light-dark cycle, temperature, humidity). Data were shared through a standardized web-based pipeline and released publicly at data.internationalbrainlab.org. All analysis code and protocols are open-source and available.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 and C261-C264 document the standardization efforts and data sharing practices. The distinction between standardized and monitored variables (C49-C50) is appropriate. The public data release and code availability (C41-C42, C261-C264) enable reproducibility and are well-documented with specific URLs and repositories.

results.result: Out of 206 mice that started training, 140 achieved proficiency in the basic task and 98 in the full task. Proficiency criteria were predefined and included performance thresholds (>80-90% on easy trials), psychometric parameters (bias <10-16%, threshold <19-20%, lapse rates <0.1-0.2), and required meeting criteria for three consecutive sessions. Two sets of criteria (1a and 1b) were used, with 1b being more stringent.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 and C74-C243 provide specific, quantitative proficiency criteria that were established before training began (C229-C230). The criteria are based on pilot data and prior work (C230), and the distinction between two criterion sets is clearly documented (C231-C232). The success rates (140/206 for basic, 98/206 for full) are transparently reported.

results.result: Four mice were excluded due to adverse effects (cataract, pain, weight loss). Of 206 mice that started training, 66 did not complete Level 1 for documented reasons: 16 died/culled (infection/illness/injury), 17 had experimental impediments, 14 failed to learn in 40 days, 12 progressed too slowly or were too old, and 7 had undocumented reasons.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C249 provide transparent accounting of all mice with specific numbers and reasons for exclusion. The documentation of exclusion criteria and reasons is thorough, though 7 mice had undocumented reasons (C249), which is a minor limitation but honestly reported.

results.result: During training, contrast threshold and bias remained relatively stable. Contrast threshold had an interquartile range of 12-29% in the first 10 days, decreasing to 11-23% thereafter (mean 17.8±11.7%). Bias ranged from -5.2% to 7.1% initially, then -5.6% to 6.5% (mean absolute bias 9.8±12.1%). Variability in performance decreased as training progressed but did not disappear.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 and C89-C92 provide specific quantitative measures of stability during training with appropriate statistical descriptors (interquartile ranges, means, standard deviations). The observation that variability decreased but persisted (C91-C92) is supported by specific data showing standard deviation decreasing from 19.1% to 10.1% between days 15-40.

results.result: A Random Forests decoder predicted slow learners (bottom quartile) with 53% accuracy (chance=25%) based on performance in the first five sessions, with only 7% chance of misclassifying fast learners as slow. There was an 80% probability of learning within 40 days, which increased with longer training duration.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 provide specific machine learning results with appropriate baseline comparisons. The modest predictive accuracy (53% vs 25% chance) and low false positive rate (7%) are honestly reported. The 80% success rate within 40 days (C95) is supported by the survival curve data.

results.result: Trial duration (stimulus onset to feedback) was 468±221 ms, showing some differences across laboratories (p=0.004, Kruskal-Wallis test). Mice performed 719±223 trials per session on average, with significant differences (p<10⁻⁶, one-way ANOVA) but only in one laboratory relative to the rest.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 report small but statistically significant differences in trial duration and session length. The statistical tests are appropriate, and the finding that only one laboratory differed in trial count (C106) suggests these differences are not systematic across all laboratories. These are minor variations that did not affect the main behavioral measures.

results.result: After correcting for slow across-trial drifts in the decision process, mice showed a win-stay/lose-switch strategy in both tasks. History-dependence was modulated by confidence in the previous trial, and perseverance could arise from slow fluctuations in decision process over trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 describe additional analyses that revealed win-stay/lose-switch behavior after correcting for slow drifts. This is supported by figure references and citations to relevant literature (C164-C165). The analysis appropriately distinguishes between different sources of history-dependence.

results.result: The manuscript contextualizes the work within the broader reproducibility crisis in neuroscience, particularly for mouse behavior. Standardized assays are common in some fields (astronomy, physics, genetics, medicine) but rarer in others (sociology, psychology, neuroscience). Previous studies have shown that mouse behavioral assays can be affected by extraneous factors and are difficult to reproduce across laboratories.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C20 and C138-C139 provide appropriate context through citations to the reproducibility literature. These are well-established facts in the field supported by multiple references. The claims accurately represent the state of the field and provide motivation for the study.

results.result: The study's approach incorporated three proposed solutions to the reproducibility crisis: large studies (5 million choices from 140 mice), many teams (seven laboratories in three countries), and upfront standardization of protocols and analyses. The collaborative, open-science nature and frequent cross-laboratory meetings may have contributed to success.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C147 accurately describe the study design features that address reproducibility concerns. The three-pronged approach (C140-C143) is well-documented in the data. The speculation about collaborative meetings contributing to success (C144, C147) is appropriately tentative and supported by a citation.

results.result: The choice of an operant behavioral task with substantial but not excessive complexity may have contributed to reproducibility success. Previous failures typically occurred with unconstrained behaviors (pain/stress responses), and operant behaviors may be inherently more reproducible. Tasks that are too simple/unconstrained or too complex/arbitrary may be harder to reproduce.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C154 are speculative (appropriately marked as such) about why this task succeeded where others failed. While the comparison to previous failures is supported by citations (C151), the claims about task complexity and reproducibility (C152-C154) are hypotheses without direct experimental support in this study. These are reasonable interpretations but remain uncertain.

results.result: The authors speculate that differences in learning times might decrease as experimenters gain experience, and suggest that full automation or individualized dynamic training methods could standardize learning rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C159 are explicitly speculative suggestions for future improvements. While supported by citations to relevant methods (C158-C159), these remain untested hypotheses in the context of this study. The speculation is appropriate for a discussion section but does not constitute supported findings.

results.result: The authors suggest future analyses could characterize behavior beyond wheel turning using videography to identify behavioral strategies. The dataset could serve as a benchmark for testing better decision-making models and investigating phenomena like lapses, block tracking, engagement states, and trial-by-trial learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C163 and C166 describe potential future uses of the data and acknowledge limitations of the current modeling approach. While the suggestions are reasonable and supported by citations to relevant methods and phenomena, these represent future work rather than current findings. The speculation is appropriate but uncertain.

results.result: The methods provide a path to training mice and reproducing behavior across laboratories, but the authors acknowledge they cannot claim this is the optimal path. Many design choices were based on intuition rather than rigorous experimentation, and it is unclear what aspects are crucial versus dispensable.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C170 provide appropriate caveats about the limitations of the work. The acknowledgment that methods were not systematically optimized (C169) and that crucial elements are unknown (C170) is honest and scientifically appropriate. This transparency about limitations is a strength.

results.result: The reproducible task is positioned as valuable for studying neural mechanisms of decision-making, analogous to standard tasks in primate research (tactile flutter, random dots). The International Brain Laboratory is using this task with neural recordings across laboratories, and other laboratories adopting the task can compare results knowing behavioral differences are unlikely.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C181 appropriately discuss implications and ongoing work. The comparison to established primate tasks (C174-C176) is supported by citations. The statement about ongoing neural recordings (C179) describes actual work in progress. The predictions about future utility (C180-C183) are reasonable extrapolations from the demonstrated behavioral reproducibility.

results.result: All procedures were approved by relevant institutional animal care committees. Mice were C57BL6/J aged 3-7 months from Jackson Laboratory or Charles River, co-housed with enrichment, kept on 12hr light-dark cycle, and fed food with 5-6% fat and 18-20% protein. Surgery involved isoflurane anesthesia, stereotaxic positioning, and headbar implantation with dental cement.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C193 provide standard methods descriptions for animal care and surgical procedures. These are straightforward factual descriptions of the experimental procedures with appropriate detail for reproducibility. The ethical approvals are properly documented (C184).

results.result: Standardized behavioral rigs included an LCD screen, 3D-printed mouse holder, steering wheel, water delivery system, photodiode for stimulus timing, environmental sensors, rotary encoder for wheel position, video camera, speaker, ultrasonic microphone, and Bpod State Machine for coordination. Task logic was programmed in Python with visual presentation in Bonsai/BonVision.
results.evaluation: Claims C194-C205 provide detailed technical specifications of the apparatus with part numbers and software versions. This level of detail supports reproducibility. The descriptions are internally consistent and supported by citations to the software packages (C204-C205).

results.result: Mice underwent water restriction or citric acid water access on weekends, followed by handling and habituation to head fixation over multiple days. Passive viewing involved Gabor stimuli at 100% contrast presented at ±35° or center with reward for center position. Active training began with wheel unlocked, 8°/mm gain, 400-700ms quiescence period, 60s response window, and feedback (reward or noise burst + timeout).
results.evaluation: Claims C206-C228 provide comprehensive procedural details for habituation and training. The progression from passive viewing to active training is logical and well-documented. Specific parameters (timing, gains, reward volumes) are provided for reproducibility. The citation supporting citric acid water use (C207) is appropriate.

results.result: In the full task, sessions began with 90 unbiased trials (50:50), then alternated between 20:80 and 80:20 blocks with length drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (mean 51, range 20-100 trials). Full task proficiency required three sessions with ≥400 trials, ≥90% correct on 100% contrast, lapses <0.1, bias >5, and median reaction time on 0% contrast >2s.
results.evaluation: Claims C250-C257 provide specific details about the full task structure and proficiency criteria. The block structure is clearly defined with specific probability values and length distributions. The proficiency criteria are quantitative and specific, enabling reproducibility.

results.result: The GLM models had low condition numbers (2.4 for basic task, 3.2 for full task), indicating they do not suffer from multicollinearity and the coefficients are interpretable.
results.evaluation: Claims C258-C260 provide appropriate statistical validation of the GLM models. Condition numbers are a standard diagnostic for multicollinearity, and the reported values (2.4 and 3.2) are indeed low, supporting the interpretation that coefficients are reliable. This is important for the validity of the modeling results.
